questions.prompt: sₙ=Σₖ₌₀ⁿ1/(k!)² and tₙ=Σₖ₌₀ⁿ binom(n,k)(−1)ᵏ/nᵏ. Which are true?
hints: Recognize tₙ by the binomial theorem.
Compare the nonnegative series defining sₙ with the exponential series.
questions.solution: The binomial theorem gives tₙ=(1−1/n)ⁿ→e^{−1}. The increasing sequence sₙ tends to S=Σₖ≥₀1/(k!)², and 2≤S<e because 1/(k!)²≤1/k!, strictly for k≥2. Consequently e^{−1}≤S and e^{−1}≤e, proving A and B. Since S<e<e², C is false; since e^{−1}<e, D is false.
questions.theory: For a bounded real sequence, its limit superior and limit inferior are the largest and smallest subsequential limiting values; for a convergent sequence both equal its limit. A series with nonnegative terms has increasing partial sums, and comparison with a convergent positive series establishes convergence and bounds on its sum. The exponential series is e=Σₖ≥₀1/k!. Factorials grow at least as fast as one, so squaring their reciprocals reduces the terms, strictly after the first two. The binomial theorem converts finite sums with binomial coefficients into powers of a two-term expression. The standard limit (1+a/n)ⁿ→eᵃ can then evaluate such powers. Establish both sequences' limits before comparing limsup and liminf statements; estimates on individual terms alone may not identify those limiting quantities.

similar_questions.prompt: Evaluate lim Σₖ₌₀ⁿbinom(n,k)2ᵏ/nᵏ.
similar_questions.solution: The binomial theorem gives (1+2/n)ⁿ, whose limit is e².

similar_questions.prompt: Show Σₖ≥₀1/(k!)³ converges and is less than e.
similar_questions.solution: Each term is at most 1/k!, strictly for k≥2. Comparison with the exponential series proves convergence and strict total bound below e.

questions.prompt: For real-valued functions fₙ on ℝ, which statements are true?

options.A: A uniform limit of uniformly continuous fₙ is uniformly continuous.
options.B: A pointwise limit of bounded fₙ is bounded.
options.C: Pointwise convergence of bounded continuous fₙ to bounded continuous f is uniform.
options.D: A uniform limit of differentiable fₙ is differentiable.

hints: Use epsilon-over-three to prove the first assertion.
For false assertions consider truncated identity functions, moving Gaussian bumps, and smooth approximations to |x|.
questions.solution: A: choose N so ‖f−f_N‖∞<ε/3, and use uniform continuity of f_N with the remaining ε/3; the triangle inequality proves uniform continuity of f. B: fₙ(x)=max(−n,min(x,n)) is bounded but tends to the unbounded identity x. C: fₙ(x)=e^{−(x−n)²} is bounded continuous and tends pointwise to zero, but sup fₙ=1. D: fₙ(x)=√(x²+1/n) is differentiable and |fₙ(x)−|x||≤1/√n, giving uniform convergence to |x|, not differentiable at zero. Only A is true.
questions.theory: Pointwise convergence controls each fixed argument separately, while uniform convergence controls the largest error over the entire domain. The supremum criterion says fₙ→f uniformly exactly when sup|fₙ−f| tends to zero. Uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous, and uniform limits of uniformly continuous functions are uniformly continuous by an epsilon-over-three argument. Uniform convergence alone does not preserve differentiability: additional control of derivatives is needed, commonly uniform convergence of derivatives plus convergence at one point. Moving bumps can tend to zero at every fixed point while retaining unit supremum, whereas narrowing bumps with shrinking heights may converge uniformly. Boundedness of each individual function does not imply a common bound or a bounded pointwise limit. Test claimed converses with explicit examples and compute a moving maximum when testing uniform convergence.

similar_questions.prompt: Does x/n converge uniformly on ℝ?
similar_questions.solution: For each fixed x, x/n→0. But sup over ℝ of |x/n| is infinite for every n, so convergence is not uniform.

similar_questions.prompt: Show sin(x)/n converges uniformly on ℝ.
similar_questions.solution: The error is at most 1/n for every x, and equals 1/n at suitable points. Its supremum tends to zero, proving uniform convergence.

questions.prompt: f is bounded and C² on (0,∞), with f″≥0. Which are true?
hints: Convexity makes f′ nondecreasing; a positive derivative would force unbounded growth.
Set g=−f′, which is nonnegative decreasing, and estimate xg(x) by a tail integral.
questions.solution: Since f′ is nondecreasing, f′(a)>0 would imply f(x)≥f(a)+(x−a)f′(a)→∞, impossible. Thus f′≤0, proving A. Its increasing limit L≤0 exists; if L<0, the function decreases at least linearly and is unbounded below, so L=0, proving B. The bounded decreasing f has a finite limit ℓ. With g=−f′ nonnegative decreasing, (x/2)g(x)≤∫_{x/2}^xg(t)dt=f(x/2)−f(x)→ℓ−ℓ=0. Hence xf′(x)→0, proving D and refuting C.
questions.theory: A twice differentiable function is convex on an interval if its second derivative is nonnegative, which implies its first derivative is nondecreasing. Supporting-line inequalities show that a positive slope on an unbounded right interval forces unbounded growth. A bounded convex function there must therefore be decreasing, with a finite limit and derivative tending to zero. The stronger estimate xf′(x)→0 uses the monotonicity of the nonnegative function g=−f′ and finite tail integrals. On [x/2,x], g(t)≥g(x), so (x/2)g(x) is bounded by that shrinking tail integral. Mere convergence of f′ to zero does not generally imply xf′ tends to zero without extra structure; convexity and boundedness supply it here. State both upper and lower boundedness when ruling out a negative limiting slope.

similar_questions.prompt: Check the conclusions for f(x)=e^{−x}.
similar_questions.solution: f is bounded, f′=−e^{−x}≤0, f″=e^{−x}>0, and both f′ and xf′ tend to zero.

similar_questions.prompt: Can f(x)=−log x be a counterexample to xf′→0 under these hypotheses?

questions.prompt: f,g are Riemann integrable on [a,b], with g([a,b])⊆[a,b]. Which are necessarily true?

options.B: If g(x)≠0 everywhere, f/g is Riemann integrable.
options.D: f∘g is Riemann integrable if both f and g are continuous.

hints: Riemann-integrable functions form an algebra, and continuous outer functions preserve integrability.
Nonvanishing without continuity need not provide a positive lower bound for |g|.
questions.solution: C is true because f²+g² is Riemann integrable and nonnegative; its bounded range permits composition with continuous square root. D follows because a composition of continuous functions is continuous and thus integrable on a compact interval. A is false on [0,1]: let f(0)=1,f(x)=0 for x>0 and let g be Thomae’s function (0 at irrationals, 1/q at a reduced rational p/q). Both are Riemann integrable but f∘g is 1 on irrationals and 0 on rationals, nowhere continuous and not integrable. B is false: f≡1, g(0)=1,g(x)=x for x>0. Then g never vanishes and is integrable, but f/g is unbounded near zero.
questions.theory: A bounded function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable exactly when its set of discontinuities has Lebesgue measure zero. Sums and products of Riemann-integrable functions remain integrable, and a continuous function composed on the outside with a Riemann-integrable function remains integrable over its bounded range. Two arbitrary Riemann-integrable functions need not have an integrable composition, because the inner function can map a large set onto a discontinuity of the outer function. A quotient is integrable if its denominator is bounded away from zero, but pointwise nonvanishing alone does not ensure this bound for a discontinuous denominator. Continuous nonzero functions on a compact interval do have such a bound by the extreme value theorem. Remember that Riemann integrability requires boundedness.

similar_questions.prompt: If f is Riemann integrable, is |f| integrable?
similar_questions.solution: Yes: the absolute-value map is continuous on the bounded range of f, so continuous composition preserves Riemann integrability.

similar_questions.prompt: Let g continuous and strictly positive on [0,1], and f integrable. Is f/g integrable?
similar_questions.solution: The extreme value theorem gives min g>0. Then 1/g is continuous and bounded, and the product f·(1/g) is Riemann integrable.

questions.prompt: Let μ be Lebesgue measure, f≥0 measurable on ℝ, and 0=a₀<a₁<a₂<⋯ be unbounded with aₙ₊₁≤caₙ for n≥1. Let Aₖ={x:aₖ≤f(x)<aₖ₊₁}. Which are true?

options.C: If Σaₖμ(Aₖ)<∞ and f≥a₁ everywhere, f is integrable.
options.D: If Σaₖμ(Aₖ)<∞ and f is bounded, f is integrable.

hints: The lower simple approximation Σaₖ1_Aₖ is bounded by f.
For k≥1 the upper approximation is at most c times the lower; the exceptional low-value region A₀ is the issue.
questions.solution: Let S=Σaₖ1_{Aₖ}. Then S≤f, so ∫S=Σaₖμ(Aₖ)≤∫f; A holds. On ⋃ₖ≥₁Aₖ, f≤cS. If f≥a₁ everywhere, A₀ is empty and ∫f≤c∫S<∞, proving C (on all ℝ those premises actually cannot occur for a strictly positive lower bound, but the implication is valid). For B and D take f≡a₁/2. It is bounded and belongs everywhere to A₀; the weighted simple function is identically zero and the series is zero, while ∫ℝf=∞. Thus neither converse nor boundedness alone controls A₀. The term a₀μ(A₀) is the integral of the zero simple-function term and is zero even on an infinite-measure set.
questions.theory: For a nonnegative measurable function, the Lebesgue integral is defined through increasing nonnegative simple-function approximations. Disjoint level sets allow the integral of a step approximation to be written as a sum of level heights times their measures. Monotonicity gives a lower integral bound whenever the step approximation is below the function. A controlled ratio between consecutive positive levels also gives an upper bound on levels above the first positive threshold. The zero-height lowest bin requires separate attention: it contributes nothing to the lower approximation while a small positive function on an infinite-measure region can still have infinite integral. Boundedness implies integrability only on a finite-measure support, not on the whole real line. Treat zero-height terms via their simple-function integrals rather than an undefined numerical product.

similar_questions.prompt: If 0≤f≤1 and f vanishes outside [0,3], prove integrability.
similar_questions.solution: The bound ∫f≤μ([0,3])=3 gives finite integral. Finite support measure supplies the missing low-value control.

similar_questions.prompt: For f≡1/2 on ℝ and dyadic levels 0,1,2,4,…, compute the lower-step integral.
similar_questions.solution: Every value is in the zero-height first bin, so the lower step is zero and its integral is zero, but the integral of f over ℝ is infinite.

questions.prompt: A nonzero C² function f:ℝ²→ℝ satisfies f(tx₁,tx₂)=t³f(x₁,x₂) for t>0. Which are necessarily true?
hints: Differentiate the homogeneity identity once and twice with respect to t at t=1.
The first derivative gives degree 3 and the second gives 3·2=6.
questions.solution: Differentiate f(tx)=t³f(x) at t=1: x₁f_x₁+x₂f_x₂=3f. At (1,−1) this is exactly B. Differentiating twice gives x₁²f_x₁x₁+2x₁x₂f_x₁x₂+x₂²f_x₂x₂=6f, proving C. A has the degree factor reversed: for f=x₁³ its left side at (1,1) is 9 and right side 1. The same f at (1,0) gives D left side 6 and right side 9, so D is false; its printed cross coefficient also differs from the homogeneity formula.
questions.theory: A function homogeneous of degree m obeys f(tx)=tᵐf(x) for positive t. Euler's homogeneous-function theorem follows by differentiating in t at one: x·∇f=mf. For a twice differentiable homogeneous function, a second derivative along the radial line gives xᵀH_f(x)x=m(m−1)f(x). The mixed Hessian entries agree under continuous second derivatives, so their contribution in two dimensions is 2x₁x₂f_x₁x₂. These identities hold without requiring f to be a polynomial. Differentiation with respect to a scaling parameter is often simpler than differentiating the first Euler identity coordinate by coordinate. For claims with wrong coefficients, a single homogeneous monomial gives an explicit counterexample. Carefully distinguish multiplying the derivative by m from multiplying the function value by m.

similar_questions.prompt: For f(x,y)=x²y, verify Euler’s identity.
similar_questions.solution: f_x=2xy and f_y=x², so xf_x+yf_y=2x²y+x²y=3f.

similar_questions.prompt: For f(x,y)=x²+y², compute xᵀH_fx.
similar_questions.solution: The Hessian is 2I. Thus the radial second derivative is 2(x²+y²)=2f, agreeing with m(m−1)=2 for degree m=2.

questions.prompt: F:M₂(ℝ)→S, where S is the symmetric matrices, is F(X)=XXᵀ. Let DF_A be its derivative at A. Which are true?

options.B: If AAᵀ=I, DF_A need not be surjective.
options.C: If A is invertible, DF_A is surjective.
options.D: If A is not invertible, DF_A is surjective.

hints: Expand F(A+H) and retain the terms linear in H.
For invertible A and symmetric B choose H=(1/2)B(Aᵀ)⁻¹.
questions.solution: F(A+H)−F(A)=HAᵀ+AHᵀ+HHᵀ, so DF_A(H)=HAᵀ+AHᵀ. If A is invertible, for symmetric B set H=(1/2)B(Aᵀ)⁻¹; then HAᵀ=B/2 and AHᵀ=B/2, yielding B. Thus C holds, and AAᵀ=I implies invertibility, proving A and refuting B. If A is singular, take nonzero v with Aᵀv=0. Every derivative output satisfies vᵀDF_A(H)v=0, whereas vᵀ(vvᵀ)v=‖v‖⁴>0. Hence it is not onto, refuting D.
questions.theory: The derivative of a map between finite-dimensional vector spaces is its linear first-order approximation, with an error that is little-o of the increment norm. For polynomial matrix maps, expansion identifies the linear terms directly, and products of two increments form a quadratic remainder. The map X↦XXᵀ always has symmetric outputs, and its derivative sends H to HAᵀ+AHᵀ. Surjectivity can be proved constructively by solving this equation for every symmetric target. If A is invertible, multiplication by its inverse gives a solution. If A is singular, a vector in the left nullspace imposes a linear restriction on every output, providing an obstruction. Surjectivity depends on the derivative at the specified base point, and should not be confused with surjectivity of the original nonlinear map.

similar_questions.prompt: Find DF_I(H) for F(X)=XXᵀ.
similar_questions.solution: At A=I the derivative is H+Hᵀ. Every symmetric B is attained by H=B/2, so it is onto the symmetric matrices.

similar_questions.prompt: Find DF_0 and decide whether it is surjective.
similar_questions.solution: The linear terms vanish at zero, so DF_0(H)=0 for every H. Its image is {0}, not the full symmetric-matrix space.

questions.prompt: On C[0,1] with supremum norm, T(f)(x)=∫₀ˣf(t)dt. Which are true?

options.A: There is α∈(0,1) with ‖Tf−Tg‖≤α‖f−g‖ for all f,g.
options.B: There is α∈(0,1) with ‖T²f−T²g‖≤α‖f−g‖ for all f,g.

hints: The constant function 1 determines ‖T‖.
Repeated integration gives a kernel with factorial decay; fixed points solve f′=f with f(0)=0.
questions.solution: ‖Tf‖≤‖f‖, and T1=x has norm 1, so ‖T‖=1 and A is false. Repeated integration yields Tⁿf(x)=1/(n−1)!∫₀ˣ(x−t)^{n−1}f(t)dt. Thus ‖Tⁿ‖≤1/n!, with equality for f≡1 at x=1. In particular ‖T²‖=1/2<1, proving B, and ‖Tⁿ‖→0, refuting D. If Tf=f, the fundamental theorem gives f′=f and f(0)=0, forcing f≡0. Hence the fixed-point set is the singleton {0}, proving C.
questions.theory: A bounded linear operator on a normed space has operator norm ‖T‖=sup_{‖f‖≤1}‖Tf‖. A strict contraction has Lipschitz constant below one; for a linear operator this is equivalent to norm below one. An operator may fail to be a contraction while one of its powers is a contraction. The Volterra integration operator gains factorial denominators under repeated integration, because integrating over ordered simplices gives the kernel (x−t)^{n−1}/(n−1)!. Upper bounds on its norm are sharp when attained by a constant function of unit norm. A fixed-point equation involving an integral can often be differentiated, but the integral also supplies an initial value at its lower endpoint. That initial value is essential for excluding nonzero solutions of the resulting differential equation.

similar_questions.prompt: For T on C[0,2], compute ‖T²‖.
similar_questions.solution: The repeated kernel gives ‖T²f‖≤(2²/2)‖f‖=2‖f‖. The constant 1 attains this at x=2, so the norm is 2.

similar_questions.solution: Differentiation gives f′=f and the equation at zero gives f(0)=1. Therefore f=eˣ, which directly satisfies the integral equation.

questions.prompt: V=ℝ[x] and f(x)=x²+x+1. Which sets are linearly independent?
hints: Expand each shifted polynomial.
Compare coefficients in a proposed zero combination; three degree-at-most-one polynomials cannot be independent.
questions.solution: f′=2x+1, f(x)−f(x−1)=2x, and f(x+1)−f(x)=2x+2. Thus A and B contain three polynomials in the two-dimensional space span{1,x}, so both are dependent. In C the three members have degrees 2,1,0; successive leading coefficients force every coefficient in a zero combination to vanish. For D suppose a(x²+3x+3)+b(x²−x+1)+c(x²+x+1)=0. Comparing coefficients gives a+b+c=0,3a−b+c=0,3a+b+c=0. Subtracting the first from the third gives a=0, then b=c=0. Hence C,D are independent.
questions.theory: A finite family is linearly independent if its only linear combination equal to zero has all coefficients zero. Polynomials of degree at most d form a vector space of dimension d+1, with basis 1,x,…,xᵈ. Expressing polynomials in that basis reduces independence to a coefficient-matrix rank calculation. Polynomials with distinct degrees are automatically independent, since the coefficient of the largest degree isolates its multiplier and one can proceed downward. Shifted copies of a polynomial share its leading coefficient but can still be independent through their lower coefficients. Finite differences of a degree-d polynomial have degree at most d−1, often explaining immediate dependence among too many differences. Equality of polynomials means equality of every coefficient, not equality merely at one chosen value of x.

similar_questions.prompt: Are x²+1,x,1 independent?
similar_questions.solution: A zero combination a(x²+1)+bx+c=0 gives a=0 from x², b=0 from x, then c=0. Thus yes.

similar_questions.prompt: Are x+1,x−1,2x independent?
similar_questions.solution: No. (x+1)+(x−1)−2x=0 is a nontrivial relation, and all three lie in a two-dimensional space.

questions.prompt: V is 3-dimensional and W is 2-dimensional over 𝔽₃. Which are true?

options.B: There are 624 surjective linear maps V→W.

hints: Each line contains exactly two nonzero vectors.
Surjective maps have two independent rows; planes are kernels of nonzero functionals modulo scalar multiples.
questions.solution: V has 3³−1=26 nonzero vectors, each line has 3−1=2, so it has 13 lines. Each plane is the kernel of a nonzero functional on V; functionals with the same kernel differ by a nonzero scalar, so there are also 26/2=13 planes. A linear map V→W is a 2×3 matrix with six independently chosen entries, giving 3⁶ maps. Surjectivity is rank two: choose the first row nonzero in 26 ways, then the second outside its 3-element span in 27−3=24 ways. The count is 26·24=624. All four statements hold.
questions.theory: An n-dimensional vector space over a finite field 𝔽_q has qⁿ vectors because each coordinate has q choices. Each one-dimensional subspace has q−1 nonzero vectors, so the number of lines is (qⁿ−1)/(q−1). Hyperplanes are kernels of nonzero linear functionals, and two such functionals have the same kernel exactly when they are nonzero scalar multiples; duality therefore gives the same hyperplane count. The operator T*T is positive semidefinite because its quadratic form is ‖Tv‖². The trace of TT* equals the sum of squared magnitudes of all entries, also known as the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm, so it vanishes only for the zero operator. A normal operator commutes with its adjoint and is unitarily diagonalizable in finite-dimensional complex inner product spaces. Self-adjoint operators are a special normal class with real eigenvalues. Spectral decomposition makes kernels of all positive powers identical for normal operators. This fails for general operators, since nilpotent Jordan blocks can annihilate a vector under a power without annihilating it in one step.

Sylvester's law of inertia states that a real quadratic form can be reduced by an invertible change of coordinates to a diagonal form with entries 1,−1,0, and the counts of these signs are invariant. A nondegenerate two-dimensional form admitting an isotropic vector must have one positive and one negative sign. Expansion of q(αv+w) normally yields a quadratic in α, but isotropy removes its squared term, leaving a nonconstant linear expression when B(v,w)≠0. Its root is therefore unique.

questions.prompt: f is entire and not a polynomial. Let A={α∈ℂ:f⁽ⁿ⁾(α)≠0 for every n≥0}. Which are true?

questions.solution: If f⁽ⁿ⁾≡0 for some n, f would be a polynomial of degree below n, contrary to hypothesis. Hence every derivative is a nonzero entire function, whose zeros are isolated. Its zero set is countable: each closed disk contains finitely many zeros, otherwise compactness gives an accumulation point and the identity theorem forces identically zero. The union over all n≥0 of these zero sets is countable. A is its complement in the uncountable set ℂ, so A is uncountable, hence infinite and nonempty. Thus A,C,D hold and B fails.
questions.theory: The identity theorem says a holomorphic function on a connected domain whose zeros have an interior accumulation point is identically zero. Thus a nonzero entire function has isolated zeros and finitely many in each compact disk, implying a countable zero set by exhaustion with integer-radius disks. Derivatives of entire functions are entire. If a sufficiently high derivative is identically zero, integrating or using Taylor coefficients shows the function is a polynomial. A nonpolynomial entire function therefore has no identically zero derivative. Countable unions of countable sets are countable, while ℂ is uncountable, so removing all derivative zero sets still leaves uncountably many points. The conclusion concerns avoiding every derivative's zeros simultaneously, not merely selecting a different nonzero point for each derivative.

Periodicity along two linearly independent directions in the complex plane reduces the entire plane to a compact fundamental parallelogram, producing global boundedness; one period alone leaves an unbounded direction and does not force constancy. The behavior of an entire function at infinity is analyzed through g(z)=f(1/z) near zero. A removable singularity there means f is bounded near infinity and hence everywhere, so f is constant. A pole corresponds exactly to a nonconstant polynomial, while a transcendental entire function has an essential singularity at infinity. The singularity classification must include all three possibilities. Do not confuse a real-periodic bounded-on-the-real-axis function with a globally bounded entire function.

Applying it to a map and its inverse proves that a disk automorphism fixing zero must be a rotation. For punctured-disk automorphisms, one must first show the removable extension fixes the missing point; merely knowing the limit lies in the closed disk is not enough. The determinant gives GL₂/SL₂≅𝔽_p×, an abelian group; every subgroup H is normal and core=H, nontrivial for |H|=2. Neither C nor D holds.

An element acts trivially on every coset exactly when it lies in every conjugate of the stabilizer subgroup, so the kernel is the core, the largest normal subgroup of G contained in H. A prime-order subgroup has no intermediate nontrivial subgroups, making triviality of its core equivalent to nonnormality. Sylow's theorems identify and conjugate subgroups whose orders are maximal prime powers dividing a finite group order. Determinant maps GL₂ over a field onto its nonzero multiplicative group, with kernel SL₂; the first isomorphism theorem identifies the quotient. Abelian groups have every subgroup normal, so a coset action with nontrivial stabilizer cannot be faithful there. The congruence class of p does not override this abelian quotient argument.

For C, multiplication M(z)=iz and conjugation C(z)=z̄ are additive group automorphisms, but C(M(z))=−iz̄ and M(C(z))=iz̄, so they do not commute. Thus only D is true.
questions.theory: An automorphism is a bijective homomorphism from a group to itself, and all automorphisms form a group under composition. For a finite group with n elements this group is contained in S_n and hence finite. Isomorphic original groups have isomorphic automorphism groups, but the converse is false: the invariant does not recover the entire group. An elementary abelian p-group is a vector space over 𝔽_p, and its group automorphisms are exactly its invertible linear transformations, giving GL_n(𝔽_p). For an additive complex group, additive automorphisms include real-linear maps such as conjugation and multiplication by nonzero complex numbers; they are not restricted to complex-linear scalar maps. To disprove abelianness, exhibit two explicit automorphisms whose compositions differ on a point.

similar_questions.prompt: Compute Aut(C₃).
similar_questions.solution: An automorphism sends a generator to either of the two generators. Thus Aut(C₃) has order 2 and is isomorphic to C₂.

similar_questions.prompt: Give noncommuting invertible maps on 𝔽₂².
similar_questions.solution: Take S=[[0,1],[1,0]] and T=[[1,1],[0,1]]. Multiplication gives ST=[[0,1],[1,1]] and TS=[[1,1],[1,0]], which differ.

questions.prompt: G₁,G₂≤G. Which are true?

options.C: If G₁◁G₂ and G₂◁G, then G₁◁G.
options.D: Every subgroup of prime index is normal.

hints: Apply the first isomorphism theorem to the natural quotient homomorphisms.
Normality is not transitive; index two is special, but an arbitrary prime index is not.
questions.solution: A follows from the map G₂→(G₂G₁)/G₁, g↦gG₁. It is onto with kernel G₂∩G₁. B follows from the surjective map (g₁,g₂)↦(g₁H₁,g₂H₂), whose kernel is H₁×H₂. C fails for G=S₄,G₂=V₄ (the identity and three double transpositions), and G₁ generated by one double transposition: G₁ is normal in abelian V₄ and V₄ is normal in S₄, but conjugation in S₄ permutes the three order-two subgroups. D fails for an order-two subgroup of S₃, of prime index 3 but not normal.
questions.theory: The first isomorphism theorem identifies a group modulo a homomorphism's kernel with its image. The second isomorphism theorem is a standard application: for N normal in G and H a subgroup, HN/N≅H/(H∩N). Product quotients are handled by applying the quotient maps componentwise; the kernel is the product of the respective kernels. Normality means invariance under conjugation by every element of the ambient group, so normality in a subgroup need not extend to a larger ambient group even if that subgroup is itself normal. Subgroups of index two are always normal because there are only two cosets, but prime indices greater than two do not ensure this. Always specify the ambient group for each normality assertion.

similar_questions.prompt: Show 2ℤ/6ℤ≅ℤ/3ℤ.
similar_questions.solution: Map 2k to k modulo 3; it is onto and has kernel 6ℤ, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the result.

similar_questions.prompt: Is the subgroup {e,(12)} normal in S₃?
similar_questions.solution: No: conjugation by (123) sends (12) to (23). Its index is 3, showing that prime index alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: f:ℚ[X]→ℚ[X] is a ring homomorphism with f(1)=1, and fⁿ is its n-fold composition. Which hold?

options.A: If f is onto, every fⁿ is onto.
options.B: ker fⁿ⁺¹=ker fⁿ for some n≥1.
options.C: If f is onto, f is one-to-one.
options.D: If f is one-to-one, f is onto.

hints: A unital homomorphism fixes every rational and is determined by h=f(X).
If h is nonconstant, substitution is injective; if h is constant, f is idempotent.
questions.solution: f fixes ℚ and has f(P)=P(h) for h=f(X). If h is nonconstant, deg P(h)=deg P·deg h for nonzero nonconstant P, so no nonzero polynomial maps to zero; f and all its powers are injective, giving identical zero kernels. If h=c∈ℚ, f is evaluation at c and f²=f, so the kernels also stabilize at n=1. This proves B. A follows by composing surjections. An onto f cannot have constant h; hence h is nonconstant and f injective, proving C (indeed onto requires degree h=1). D fails for h=X²: substitution is injective, but every image has only even powers and X is absent.
questions.theory: A unital endomorphism of a polynomial ring over ℚ fixes the rational constants: additivity fixes integers and multiplicativity preserves their inverses. The universal property of a polynomial ring therefore says it is completely determined by the image h of X, with action P↦P(h). Composition of nonconstant polynomials multiplies degrees, so substitution by a nonconstant polynomial is injective. Surjectivity requires h of degree one, since an image equal to X forces degree P times degree h to equal one. Constant substitution is an evaluation homomorphism with principal kernel (X−c) and is idempotent. More generally polynomial rings over fields are Noetherian and ascending chains of ideals stabilize, explaining eventual kernel stabilization of endomorphism iterates. Injectivity and surjectivity of an infinite set map are distinct properties.

similar_questions.prompt: Is P(X)↦P(3X+2) an automorphism of ℚ[X]?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Its inverse substitutes (X−2)/3, so it is bijective.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the kernels of all positive powers of evaluation at X=4.
similar_questions.solution: Evaluation is idempotent because rational outputs are fixed. Every positive power has kernel (X−4).

questions.prompt: f(X)=X⁵+X+1 and g(X)=X⁵−X+1 in ℚ[X]. Which are true?

options.A: f is irreducible but g is not.
options.B: g is irreducible but f is not.

hints: Factor f using the cyclotomic factor X²+X+1.
Reduce g modulo 3 and exclude linear and irreducible quadratic divisors.
questions.solution: f=(X²+X+1)(X³−X²+1), so it is reducible. Modulo 3, g=X⁵+2X+1 has value 1 at each of 0,1,2, so it has no linear factor. The monic irreducible quadratics over 𝔽₃ are X²+1, X²+X+2, X²+2X+2. Division of g gives remainders 1, X+1, X+1 respectively, none zero. A reducible degree-five polynomial must have an irreducible factor of degree at most two; otherwise every factor degree is at least three and their sum exceeds five. Thus g is irreducible modulo 3. As g is monic with integer coefficients, Gauss’s lemma and reduction prove irreducibility over ℚ. Only B holds.
questions.theory: A polynomial over a field is irreducible when it cannot be factored into two positive-degree polynomials. For a primitive integer polynomial, Gauss's lemma equates reducibility over ℚ with reducibility over ℤ. If its leading coefficient survives reduction modulo a prime and the reduced polynomial is irreducible, the original is irreducible over ℚ. Degree determines what factors must be checked: a reducible degree-five polynomial has a factor of degree one or two, while excluding rational roots alone does not suffice. Over a small finite field one can list all monic irreducible quadratics and compute division remainders. A successful explicit factorization immediately proves reducibility. The modular test is one-directional: reducibility modulo a particular prime does not imply reducibility over ℚ.

similar_questions.prompt: Prove X³+X+1 is irreducible over ℚ.
similar_questions.solution: Modulo 2 it has no roots: values at 0 and 1 are both 1. A cubic over a field is reducible iff it has a root, so the reduction is irreducible; Gauss’s lemma proves the claim.

similar_questions.prompt: Why does no rational root not prove irreducibility for a quartic?
similar_questions.solution: (X²+1)(X²+2)=X⁴+3X²+2 has no real, hence no rational, root but has a nontrivial quadratic factorization.

questions.prompt: p>2 is prime and 𝔽̄_p is an algebraic closure. Which hold?

options.A: For f∈𝔽_p[X] and a root α, 𝔽_p(α) is its splitting field.
options.B: For irreducible f,g of the same degree and a root α of f, 𝔽_p(α) is a splitting field of g.
options.C: 𝔽_p[X] has infinitely many irreducible polynomials.

hints: Finite fields of a given size are unique inside an algebraic closure.
The set of squares has (p+1)/2 elements, so it meets its translate reflected about any target.
questions.solution: A is false: choose a nonsquare d∈𝔽_p and f=X(X²−d), with root α=0. Then 𝔽_p(α)=𝔽_p lacks the other roots. For B, irreducible degree d gives 𝔽_p(α)=𝔽_{pᵈ}; every irreducible polynomial of degree d splits in this unique field, and its roots generate it. C follows by Euclid's argument: if r₁,…,r_k were all monic irreducibles, the nonconstant polynomial Xr₁⋯r_k+1 would have an irreducible divisor not among them. For D, let Q be the square set, of size (p+1)/2. For any c∈𝔽_p, Q and c−Q have total size p+1 and must intersect. Thus c=a²+b². The left set is all 𝔽_p, so D holds.
questions.theory: Finite fields of size pᵈ exist for every positive integer d and are unique as subfields of an algebraic closure, consisting of roots of X^{pᵈ}−X. An irreducible degree-d polynomial over 𝔽_p has its roots in 𝔽_{pᵈ}, with the Frobenius automorphism cycling them, and any root generates that field. For a general reducible polynomial, a single root need not generate a field containing all other roots. Polynomial rings over fields have infinitely many monic irreducibles by a product-plus-one argument analogous to Euclid's prime proof. In an odd finite field, every nonzero square has exactly two square roots, giving (p+1)/2 squares including zero. A pigeonhole intersection then represents every field element as a sum of two squares, regardless of whether it is itself a square.

similar_questions.prompt: Represent every element of 𝔽₃ as a sum of two squares.
similar_questions.solution: Squares are 0 and 1. We have 0=0+0,1=1+0,2=1+1, covering all elements.

similar_questions.prompt: If α is a root of an irreducible cubic over 𝔽₅, what is |𝔽₅(α)|?
similar_questions.solution: The extension degree is 3, so the field has 5³=125 elements and contains all roots of every irreducible cubic over 𝔽₅.

questions.prompt: p:ℝ→ℝ is a nonconstant polynomial. Which are true?

options.A: Preimages of compact sets under p are compact.
options.B: Preimages of connected sets under p are connected.
options.C: At every point p restricts on some open neighborhood to a homeomorphism onto an open set.
options.D: Images of bounded sets under p are bounded.

hints: Nonconstant polynomials have |p(x)|→∞ as |x|→∞.
Use p(x)=x² for the connectedness and local-homeomorphism claims.
questions.solution: A compact K is closed and bounded. Continuity makes p⁻¹(K) closed, and |p(x)|→∞ ensures it is bounded. By Heine–Borel it is compact, proving A. If E is bounded it lies in [−M,M], and continuity bounds p on that compact interval, proving D. B fails for p=x² and K={1}: the preimage is {−1,1}, disconnected though K is connected. C fails for x² at 0, since every open neighborhood contains ±ε with the same image, so no restriction there is injective or a homeomorphism.
questions.theory: A continuous map sends compact sets to compact sets, but its preimages of compact sets need not generally be compact. A map with compact preimages is called proper; a nonconstant real polynomial is proper because its absolute value tends to infinity at both ends of the real line. In ℝ, Heine–Borel identifies compactness with being closed and bounded. Connected subsets of ℝ are intervals, but continuity preserves connectedness under images rather than arbitrary preimages. A local homeomorphism must be injective on a neighborhood and map that neighborhood onto an open set. Critical turning points of polynomials can prevent this property. To bound an image of a bounded nonclosed set, enclose the set in a compact interval and use continuity there.

similar_questions.prompt: Find p⁻¹([1,4]) for p(x)=x² and test compactness.
similar_questions.solution: It is [−2,−1]∪[1,2], closed and bounded, hence compact, but disconnected.

similar_questions.prompt: Is x³ a local homeomorphism at zero despite derivative zero?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. It is globally strictly increasing, bijective, and has continuous inverse cube root. A nonzero derivative is sufficient, not necessary, for a local homeomorphism.

questions.prompt: S={a+b√2:a,b∈ℚ}⊂ℝ has the subspace topology. Which are true?

options.C: S\ℚ is discrete in the subspace topology on S.

hints: S contains ℚ, and S\ℚ contains √2+ℚ.
Both are dense, while S is countable and contains more than one point.
questions.solution: S contains ℚ, so its closure is ℝ, proving A. Every √2+q with q∈ℚ is irrational and lies in S; translating a dense set preserves density, so B holds. C is false: for any s∈S\ℚ, the points s+1/n also belong to S\ℚ, are distinct from s, and converge to it, so no point is isolated. S is countable because ℚ² is countable. A connected subset of ℝ with two different points must contain the interval between them, which is uncountable. Since S includes 0 and 1 but is countable, it is not connected; D fails.
questions.theory: A subset of ℝ is dense if every nonempty open interval contains one of its points. Supersets and translates of dense sets are dense, so rational subsets often provide easy density proofs. A discrete subspace is one where each point is isolated relative to that subspace; arbitrarily close distinct points or a convergent sequence within the set disproves discreteness. Connected subsets of the real line are exactly intervals, including singleton intervals. A countable subset containing at least two points therefore cannot be connected, because the interval joining those points is uncountable. Density does not imply connectedness: ℚ itself is the standard counterexample. In a rational span involving an irrational number, a nonzero irrational coefficient ensures irrationality, and adding a rational number preserves it.

similar_questions.prompt: Is √3+ℚ dense in ℝ and discrete?
similar_questions.solution: It is a translate of ℚ, hence dense. For any point s, s+1/n stays in the set and converges to s, so it is not discrete.

similar_questions.prompt: Is ℚ connected in its subspace topology?
similar_questions.solution: No. Splitting at an irrational number such as √2 gives two nonempty relatively open sets ℚ∩(−∞,√2) and ℚ∩(√2,∞) that separate it.

questions.prompt: D=[−1,1]² and f(x,y)=1+√(y₊), y₊=max(y,0). For y′=f(x,y), y(0)=0, which are true?

options.A: f is Lipschitz continuous on D.
options.B: f is not Lipschitz continuous on D.
options.C: The IVP has at least one solution.

hints: Compare f(0,t) and f(0,0) as t tends down to zero.
Continuity alone gives local existence by Peano’s theorem.
questions.solution: For t>0, |f(0,t)−f(0,0)|/t=√t/t=1/√t→∞, so no finite Lipschitz constant exists; B holds and A fails. But f is continuous on the rectangle and the initial point is interior. Peano’s existence theorem gives at least one local solution, proving C and refuting D. An explicit construction uses y=x for x≤0 near zero, and for x≥0 the increasing inverse of x=∫₀ʸds/(1+√s)=2√y−2log(1+√y). Both pieces meet with derivative 1 at zero and remain in D on a sufficiently small interval.
questions.theory: Peano's existence theorem guarantees a local solution to y′=f(x,y) when f is continuous near the initial point. The Picard–Lindelöf theorem adds local Lipschitz continuity in y to guarantee uniqueness, but this stronger hypothesis is sufficient rather than necessary. A square-root nonlinearity is continuous yet fails Lipschitz continuity at zero because its difference quotient grows like the inverse square root. Failure of a Lipschitz condition does not mean that solutions do not exist. An autonomous equation y′=F(y) with positive continuous F can be solved locally by integrating dx/dy=1/F(y) and inverting the strictly increasing resulting function. Domain restrictions on the rectangle control how long the local solution remains valid. Distinguish existence from uniqueness and local from global conclusions.

similar_questions.prompt: Does y′=√|y|, y(0)=0 have a solution?
similar_questions.solution: Yes: y≡0 solves it. There are also delayed positive solutions y=(x−a)²/4 for x≥a and zero before a, showing that non-Lipschitz continuity can permit nonuniqueness.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve y′=1+y, y(0)=0.
similar_questions.solution: Separation or a linear integrating factor gives y=eˣ−1. The right side is Lipschitz in y, so this solution is locally unique.

questions.prompt: φ₁,φ₂ solve y″+cos(x)y′+sin(x)y=0 with (φ₁(0),φ₁′(0))=(1,0) and (φ₂(0),φ₂′(0))=(0,1). Which hold?
hints: Shifts by integer periods preserve the differential equation.
The two initial-value-normalized solutions form a basis of the two-dimensional solution space.
questions.solution: Both coefficients have period 2π. Substitution shows a solution shifted by 2π or 4π satisfies the same equation, proving A,B. The Wronskian at zero is 1·1−0·0=1, so φ₁,φ₂ are a fundamental system. Every other solution, including either shifted one, is a constant linear combination of them. Explicitly any solution ψ has ψ=ψ(0)φ₁+ψ′(0)φ₂ by initial-value uniqueness. Hence D holds and C is false. Periodic coefficients do not require the individual solutions themselves to be periodic.
questions.theory: A homogeneous linear second-order ODE with continuous coefficients has a two-dimensional solution space, and each pair of initial value and derivative determines a unique solution. Two solutions form a fundamental system when their Wronskian is nonzero at some point. Abel's identity then makes the Wronskian nonzero everywhere on the interval. If the equation's coefficients are periodic with period P, shifting a solution by P again gives a solution, because the shifted coefficients coincide. In a fixed fundamental basis this shift is represented by a constant monodromy matrix. The new solution is therefore a linear combination of the old basis, although it need not equal the original solution or be periodic itself. The distinction between periodic coefficients and periodic solutions is central to such questions.

similar_questions.prompt: For y″+y=0 with basis cos x,sin x, express cos(x+a).
similar_questions.solution: The addition formula gives cos(x+a)=cos a cos x−sin a sin x, a constant linear combination.

similar_questions.prompt: Can y″−y=0 have periodic coefficients and nonperiodic solutions?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Its constant coefficients are periodic with any period, while eˣ and e^{−x} are nonperiodic solutions.

questions.prompt: For continuous q on ℝ, consider y″+q(x)y=0. Which existence statements are FALSE?

options.A: Some q admits both cos x and eˣcos x as solutions.
options.B: Some q admits both sin x and cos x as solutions.
options.C: Some q admits both eˣsin x and eˣcos(2x) as solutions.
options.D: Some q admits both xeˣ and x(x−1)eˣ as solutions.

C is impossible already for eˣsin x: at zero its value is 0 but its second derivative is 2, contradicting the ODE. questions.theory: For y″+q(x)y=0 with continuous q, every solution is twice continuously differentiable and its second derivative vanishes at every zero of y. This follows immediately from the equation and is a quick compatibility test for proposed solutions. Away from zeros, a nonzero candidate determines q=−y″/y; continuity must extend this expression through zeros without a singularity. Two candidate solutions must therefore give the same q on their nonzero sets and compatible behavior at their zeros. Abel's identity also says their Wronskian is constant because the y′ coefficient is zero. A proposed pair with nonconstant Wronskian cannot be a fundamental pair for such an equation. Check the simplest point or zero before attempting a complicated global coefficient calculation.

similar_questions.prompt: Can y=x be a solution of y″+q(x)y=0 on ℝ?
similar_questions.solution: Yes, q≡0 works because y″=0. Away from zero the equation forces q=0, and continuity then fixes q(0)=0.

similar_questions.prompt: Can y=x² be a solution with q continuous on ℝ?
similar_questions.solution: No. At zero y=0 but y″=2, so the differential equation would require 2=0.

questions.prompt: For xuₓ+uᵧ=1 with u(0,y)=eʸ, which hold?

options.A: There is no neighborhood of the origin on which a solution exists.
options.B: There is a unique solution on some neighborhood of the origin.
options.C: There is a unique solution on some neighborhood of (0,1).
options.D: There are infinitely many solutions each on some neighborhood of the origin.

hints: On the initial line x=0 the PDE reduces to uᵧ=1.
Differentiate the prescribed trace eʸ along that same line.
questions.solution: Any classical solution near a segment of x=0 must satisfy uᵧ(0,y)=1 by the PDE. But differentiating u(0,y)=eʸ gives uᵧ(0,y)=eʸ. Equality holds only at y=0, not on any open segment around zero. Every neighborhood of the origin contains points (0,y) with y≠0, so no solution exists there, proving A and refuting B,D. At (0,1) the two values already differ, e≠1, refuting C. The initial line is characteristic, and its assigned data violate the required tangential evolution.
questions.theory: For a first-order PDE a uₓ+b uᵧ=c, characteristics have tangent vector (a,b). Initial data on a curve determine a standard locally unique Cauchy problem only when that vector is transverse to the curve. If the curve is characteristic, its trace cannot be prescribed arbitrarily; the PDE restricts the derivative of that trace along the curve. On x=0 for the vector field (x,1), the characteristic direction is vertical, so the trace must have derivative one in y. Data agreeing with that derivative at a single point are insufficient for a solution on an open neighborhood, which includes a whole curve segment. Incompatible characteristic data give nonexistence, while compatible data may allow nonuniqueness. Always test tangential compatibility before invoking a Cauchy existence theorem.

similar_questions.prompt: For xuₓ+uᵧ=1, is the trace u(0,y)=y+C compatible?
similar_questions.solution: Yes: its y derivative is 1, matching the PDE on the characteristic line. For example u=y+C is a global solution.

similar_questions.prompt: Find multiple solutions with that compatible trace.
similar_questions.solution: u=y+C+F(xe^{−y}) satisfies xuₓ+uᵧ=1 for any differentiable F with F(0)=0. Thus infinitely many solutions share the trace.

questions.prompt: u solves uₓₓ+uᵧᵧ+uₓ=0 in x²+y²<1, with boundary values u=1+2x²y² on x²+y²=1. Which hold?
hints: Apply the maximum and minimum principles for an elliptic equation with drift and no zeroth-order term.
On the boundary set s=x², so y²=1−s.
questions.solution: The operator Δ+∂ₓ is uniformly elliptic, with no zeroth-order term. The maximum and minimum principles put extrema of the continuous solution on the closed disk at the boundary. There x²+y²=1 and x²y²=s(1−s) for s∈[0,1]. Its minimum is zero (at axis endpoints) and maximum is 1/4 (when x²=y²=1/2). Boundary values therefore range from 1 to 1+2·1/4=3/2. They are attained, yielding A,D. The drift term does not alter the boundary-extremum conclusion. Over the open interior alone the strong principle gives strict inequalities, with these boundary values as infimum and supremum.
questions.theory: A uniformly elliptic linear operator has a positive-definite principal coefficient matrix with a uniform lower eigenvalue bound. The operator Δ+b·∇ has the identity as that matrix and a first-order drift term. With no positive zeroth-order coefficient, its maximum principle bounds a classical solution continuous up to a bounded domain's boundary by its boundary extrema; applying it to −u gives the minimum bound. The strong principle prohibits interior extrema for a nonconstant solution. Boundary optimization is then an ordinary constrained algebra problem. On a unit circle, x²y²≤[(x²+y²)/2]²=1/4 by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, and equality is achievable. questions.prompt: Suppose ∫₀³f(x)dx=(3/2)[f(α)+f(α+β)] for every polynomial of degree ≤2. Which are true?

questions.solution: Let r=α and s=α+β. The constant condition is automatic: 3=(3/2)·2. For f=x, 9/2=(3/2)(r+s), so r+s=3. For f=x², 9=(3/2)(r²+s²), so r²+s²=6 and rs=[9−6]/2=3/2. Thus nodes solve t²−3t+3/2=0 and are (3±√3)/2. Either ordering is allowed, giving β=s−r=±√3 and exactly the pairs in A. questions.theory: A quadrature formula approximates an integral by a weighted sum of values at chosen nodes. Its degree of exactness is the largest degree for which it integrates every polynomial exactly. By linearity, exactness for all polynomials through degree d is equivalent to matching the moments of the basis 1,x,…,xᵈ. For two equal-weight nodes, the first two nonconstant moment equations determine their sum and sum of squares, and hence their product. Solving the associated quadratic gives the nodes, with swapping them leaving the formula unchanged. These are the two-point Gauss–Legendre nodes after scaling an interval from [−1,1]. Do not interpret β as a node: the second node is α+β, so reversing the node order changes the sign of β.

At α=3 this is (x⁴+14)/15; at α=1 it is (x²+2)/3; at α=0 it is x. Thus A,B,C hold. questions.theory: For a fixed-endpoint variational problem with integrand depending only on x and y′, the Euler–Lagrange equation reduces to conservation of F_y′. In a weighted Dirichlet energy ∫w(x)(y′)²dx with positive continuous weight w, this implies wy′ is constant. The resulting extremal is obtained by integrating 1/w and normalizing to the endpoint displacement. Positivity of the weight also makes the functional strictly convex on the admissible affine space, so the extremal is the unique minimizer. An alternative derivation uses Cauchy–Schwarz: the fixed displacement ∫y′ bounds the energy, with equality when y′ is proportional to 1/w. Satisfying endpoints alone does not identify an extremal; the differential stationarity condition must also hold.

questions.solution: For an admissible stationary y and perturbation h with h(0)=h(1)=0, expansion gives J[y+h]−J[y]=δJ[y](h)+∫₀²[a(h′)²+2bhh′+ch²]dx; the first term is zero by extremality. In B the remaining integrand is (h′)²+2h²>0 for nonzero h. In C it is 2(h′−h/2)²+h²/2, and in D it is (h′−2h)²+h². Both are positive definite, so every admissible extremal is a strict global minimizer. In A it is −2(h′−h/2)²−3h²/2, negative for nonzero h, so any stationary extremal is a maximum, not a minimum. Thus B,C,D hold. The source’s interval [0,2] and interior constraint at x=1 are kept literally; no assumption that y(2) is fixed is needed because stationarity, including any required natural condition, eliminates the first variation. Official-key discrepancy: the NTA final key for exact ID562954174 lists ABCD. This cannot be explained by changing a sign in the displayed integrand: A is strictly concave, and whenever an admissible stationary point exists, a nonzero smooth perturbation supported away from 0 and1 decreases J, so that point is not a minimizer. The literal interior constraint creates a further regularity ambiguity. In a usual piecewise-smooth or Sobolev class, stationarity can allow a derivative jump at1 and the negative-definite problem has a maximum. If instead only globally C1 or C2 candidates are allowed, the Euler equation plus values at0,1 and the natural condition at2 can be overdetermined; absence of stationary candidates makes “every admissible extremal” vacuously true. The source does not specify this class. Therefore this entry records the genuine source/key ambiguity and conditional BCD classification instead of silently adopting ABCD or changing y(1) to y(2).
questions.theory: A quadratic functional has an exact expansion under y↦y+h: a linear first-variation term plus a quadratic remainder in h and h′. At an admissible extremal the first variation vanishes for every admissible perturbation. If the quadratic remainder is positive for every nonzero perturbation, the extremal is a strict global minimum; if negative, it is a strict maximum. For an integrand a(h′)²+2bhh′+ch², positive definiteness of the symmetric matrix [[a,b],[b,c]] is ensured by a>0 and ac−b²>0. Completing squares verifies this directly. Endpoint or interior constraints determine which perturbations are allowed, and free endpoints introduce natural boundary conditions into stationarity. The positivity argument works regardless of that placement once stationarity holds; treating a mixed term as a fixed boundary constant requires that both corresponding endpoint values actually be fixed.

similar_questions.prompt: At a stationary point of ∫[(y′)²−2yy′+2y²]dx, classify it using variations.
similar_questions.solution: The quadratic remainder is (h′−h)²+h², strictly positive for a nonzero perturbation. Hence the stationary point is a strict global minimum.

similar_questions.prompt: Classify a stationary point of −∫[(y′)²+y²]dx.
similar_questions.solution: The remainder is −∫[(h′)²+h²], negative for every nonzero h. Thus the stationary point is a strict maximum and not a minimum.

hints: Differentiate the Volterra equation three times.
The equation becomes u‴=8u, with u(0)=u′(0)=0,u″(0)=2.
questions.solution: Differentiation gives u′=2x+8∫₀ˣ(x−t)u(t)dt, u″=2+8∫₀ˣu(t)dt, and u‴=8u. The initial data are 0,0,2. The characteristic roots are 2,−1±i√3. Solving for constants gives u(x)=(1/6)[e^{2x}−e^{−x}(cos√3x+√3sin√3x)]. At zero this is 0. At x=2π/√3 the cosine is 1 and sine 0, yielding B. At x=π/(2√3) the cosine is 0 and sine 1, yielding C. D has both an incorrect sign and decay exponent. Thus A,B,C hold; the differentiated equation with its initial data is equivalent to the original integral equation by integrating back three times.
questions.theory: A Volterra integral equation integrates only up to the free variable x, so differentiating it uses Leibniz's rule and creates endpoint terms. For a polynomial kernel (x−t)ᵐ, successive derivatives lower the degree until the next derivative exposes u(x). The equation becomes a linear ODE of order m+1, with initial derivatives determined at the integral's lower endpoint. Constant-coefficient ODEs are solved through their characteristic polynomial; complex conjugate roots produce real exponential sine and cosine terms. One must retain all initial conditions to make the differentiated problem equivalent to the integral equation, since differentiation alone can lose integration constants. After obtaining a formula, special arguments may simplify the trigonometric factors. Track factors of m! and the original kernel multiplier carefully.

questions.prompt: Let f,K be such that the solution of y″−3y′+2y=4sin x, y(0)=1,y′(0)=−2 satisfies y(x)=f(x)+∫₀ˣK(x,t)y(t)dt. Which hold?

questions.solution: Literal issue: merely requiring one fixed solution y to satisfy a Volterra equation does not determine f and K. For instance K≡0,f=y always works. Thus no displayed value of f is forced without specifying the canonical ODE-to-integral-equation conversion. Under that intended conversion, twice integrate y″=3y′−2y+4sin x to obtain y=1−2x+∫₀ˣ(x−t)[3y′(t)−2y(t)+4sin t]dt. Integration by parts gives ∫₀ˣ(x−t)y′(t)dt=−x+∫₀ˣy(t)dt, while ∫₀ˣ(x−t)sin t dt=x−sin x. Hence f=1−x−4sin x and K=3−2(x−t). Then f′=−1−4cos x, f′(π)=3, f(π)+f′(π)=4−π, and f(0)+f′(0)=−4, giving conditional A,B,D. To demonstrate literal nonuniqueness explicitly, the IVP solution is y=2eˣ−(11/5)e^{2x}+(2/5)sin x+(6/5)cos x; the allowed choice f=y,K=0 does not satisfy f′(π)=3 or f(0)+f′(0)=−4 (its latter sum is −1).
questions.theory: A second-order IVP can be put into a canonical Volterra equation by integrating twice from the initial point and using the initial value and derivative. The identity y(x)=y(0)+xy′(0)+∫₀ˣ(x−t)y″(t)dt provides the starting point. Derivative terms inside the integral are removed by integration by parts, placing them into the kernel and the initial-data contribution. This construction is equivalent to the ODE if its derived f and K are retained. However, a statement that a single solution satisfies some Volterra equation does not uniquely recover f and K: changing the kernel and adjusting f preserves the same solution. Numerical claims about f therefore require a normalization or explicit formula. Distinguish an intended canonical conversion from unrestricted existence of an integral representation.

similar_questions.prompt: Convert y″=2y, y(0)=1,y′(0)=0 to its canonical Volterra equation.
similar_questions.solution: Twice integration gives y(x)=1+2∫₀ˣ(x−t)y(t)dt. Thus f=1,K=2(x−t); differentiating twice and retaining initial data reverses the conversion.

similar_questions.prompt: Show nonuniqueness of a representation for y≡1.

questions.prompt: For smooth phase-space functions f,g depending on coordinates qᵢ,momenta pᵢ,time t, write [f,g] for their Poisson bracket and H for the Hamiltonian. Which hold?

options.B: If f is a constant of motion independent of t, [H,f] is a constant of motion.
options.D: If f,g are constants of motion, [f,g] is a constant of motion.

hints: The Poisson bracket is bilinear and obeys the Jacobi identity.
Along Hamiltonian flow use Df=∂ₜf+[f,H].
questions.solution: A follows by the product rule applied to [f,g]=Σ(f_qᵢg_pᵢ−f_pᵢg_qᵢ). If f is time-independent and conserved, 0=Df=[f,H], so [H,f]=0 and is conserved, proving B. C is precisely the Jacobi identity. For D, the time product rule and Jacobi identity give D[f,g]=[Df,g]+[f,Dg]. If Df=Dg=0, this derivative vanishes. Hence all four hold, including explicitly time-dependent integrals of motion in D.
questions.theory: The canonical Poisson bracket of smooth functions is [f,g]=Σ(∂f/∂qᵢ·∂g/∂pᵢ−∂f/∂pᵢ·∂g/∂qᵢ). It is antisymmetric, bilinear, obeys a product rule, and satisfies the Jacobi identity, making phase-space functions a Lie algebra. Hamilton's equations imply the total derivative along motion is Df=∂ₜf+[f,H]. A constant of motion has Df=0, which differs from having no explicit time dependence. The partial time derivative distributes over the bracket because canonical coordinates are held fixed and mixed derivatives commute. The Hamiltonian derivative is also a derivation of the bracket by Jacobi, so the bracket of two conserved quantities is conserved. Sign conventions can reverse every bracket, but these structural identities remain valid when used consistently.

similar_questions.solution: p has no explicit time dependence and [p,H]=−H_q=0. Thus Dp=0; its powers are conserved as well.

A Poisson variable with rate ν has characteristic function E(e^{itX})=exp[ν(e^{it}−1)], obtained from its exponential generating series. Characteristic functions of independent sums multiply. A jump of size F(a)−F(a−) is the probability mass at a, while a derivative on a smooth interval gives its density there. Expectations then combine a discrete weighted sum with an integral over the continuous part. The moment-generating function similarly includes both pieces: E(e^{tX}). In this finite chain the only closed class is {5}, so its point mass is the unique stationary distribution. State 1 has positive-probability return paths 1→3→4→1 (length 3) and 1→2→3→4→1 (length 4), whose gcd is 1. All communicating states 1–4 share period 1. State 5 has a one-step loop and period 1. In a finite Markov chain, closed irreducible classes are recurrent, while states outside them are transient; stationary distributions put mass only on closed classes. An absorbing state has self-transition probability one and is a closed singleton class. The period of a state is the greatest common divisor of all positive possible return times, and communicating states have the same period, even in a transient class. A self-loop is sufficient but not necessary for aperiodicity: two return lengths with gcd one also establish period one. Distinguish p_ii⁽ⁿ⁾, which starts at i, from the probability of being at i from an arbitrary initial distribution.

Use the law of large numbers for Tₙ/n,Vₙ/n and Slutsky’s theorem.
questions.solution: The CLT yields Sₙ/√n⇒N(0,1), proving A. For squared observations, mean is 1 and variance 3−1=2, so (Tₙ−n)/√(2n)⇒N(0,1); division by √(3n) instead yields N(0,2/3), refuting B. Since Tₙ/n→1 in probability, √nSₙ/Tₙ=(Sₙ/√n)/(Tₙ/n)⇒N(0,1), proving C. Since Vₙ/n→3, the last ratio converges to N(0,2/3), refuting D. On any rare event Tₙ=0, a ratio can be defined arbitrarily; its probability tends to zero by the law of large numbers.
questions.theory: The classical iid central limit theorem needs finite variance and centers the sum by n times its mean, then scales by the square root of n times its variance. Applying it to a transformed variable requires computing that variable's own variance: for X², it is EX⁴−(EX²)². The law of large numbers gives sample averages convergence in probability when the corresponding first absolute moment is finite. Slutsky's theorem permits multiplication or division of a distributionally convergent variable by a random quantity tending in probability to a nonzero constant. Random normalization must converge to the correct variance scale; an uncentered fourth-moment average estimates EX⁴ rather than Var(X²). Merely having the same order √n does not make two normalizations equivalent.

questions.prompt: X,Y are iid N(0,1), S=X²+Y² and T=e^{−(X²+Y²)/2}. Which hold?

questions.solution: S~χ²₂, equivalently exponential with rate 1/2, so A holds and Var S=2·2=4, refuting C. For 0<t<1, P(T≤t)=P(S≥−2log t)=exp[−(−2log t)/2]=t. Thus T is uniform on (0,1), proving B. Its mean is 1/2, not 2/3, refuting D.
questions.theory: A chi-square variable with k degrees of freedom is the sum of squares of k independent standard normal variables. Its mean is k and variance 2k. For k=2 its density simplifies to (1/2)e^{−s/2}, an exponential distribution. Monotone transformations can be studied with CDFs: a decreasing transformation reverses the event inequality, so use the original survival probability. If S has an exponential distribution with rate λ, then e^{−λS} is uniform on (0,1), a version of the probability integral transform. This does not depend on a separate normalization constant once λ is correctly identified. Confusing the chi-square mean with its variance is a common error; the variance has the additional factor of two.

similar_questions.prompt: If E~Exp(rate 3), find the distribution of e^{−3E}.

similar_questions.prompt: For a sum of five independent squared standard normals, find mean and variance.

hints: Count exactly how many independent squared normals occur in each denominator.
questions.solution: X−Y+1 is normal with mean zero and variance 4+9−2·3=7. Ten independent terms, divided by √7, therefore give N(0,10), proving A. X+Y−11 has variance 4+9+6=19, so its ten squared standardized copies sum to χ²₁₀, proving B. For C, write Zᵢ=(Xᵢ−5)/2. The ratio is √8 Z₁/√(Σᵢ₌₃¹⁰Zᵢ²); the denominator sum has 8 terms, independent of Z₁, giving t₈, not t₉. In D the standardized numerator and denominator sums are independent χ²₃ and χ²₆; 2 times their ratio equals (χ²₃/3)/(χ²₆/6), giving F_{3,6}.
questions.theory: Linear combinations of jointly normal variables are normal, with variance obtained from all individual variances and covariance cross terms. A sum of squared independent standard normals has a chi-square law with degrees of freedom equal to the number of terms. A t variable is Z/√(U/ν), where Z is standard normal and U is independent chi-square with ν degrees of freedom. An F variable is (U/r)/(V/s) for independent chi-square variables with r and s degrees of freedom. Independent sample pairs make variables from disjoint observation indices independent even when X and Y within the same pair are correlated. Count index ranges inclusively, and divide squared deviations by their known variance before invoking these distribution identities.

similar_questions.prompt: If Z is standard normal and U is independent χ²₄, identify 2Z/√U.

similar_questions.prompt: Independent U~χ²₂,V~χ²₅ are given. Identify (5U)/(2V).

questions.prompt: Xᵢ are iid with density e^{−(x−θ)} for x≥θ, θ∈ℝ. Let Y=min Xᵢ. Which intervals have confidence coefficient 1−α, 0<α<1?
hints: The pivot W=n(Y−θ) has Exp(1) law.

questions.solution: P(Y−θ>t)=e^{−nt}, so W=n(Y−θ)~Exp(1). For D, coverage requires −log(1−α/2)<W<−log(α/2), of probability (1−α/2)−α/2=1−α. For C the bounds double, giving probability (1−α/2)²−(α/2)²=1−α, so it is also valid. For A the upper endpoint exceeds Y≥θ, and coverage reduces to W<−log(1−α/2), with probability α/2, not the required coefficient in general. B gives W<−(1/2)logα, with probability 1−√α, not 1−α. Thus C,D are valid for all stated α.
questions.theory: For a shifted exponential sample, the minimum is the shift plus an exponential waiting time with rate n: independence multiplies the n survival probabilities. Multiplying that excess by n gives a parameter-free rate-one exponential pivot. A confidence interval's coverage is obtained by rearranging its endpoints into inequalities for this pivot and then subtracting exponential survival probabilities. Equal-tail central intervals are one construction, but they are not the only intervals with a specified coverage. Different endpoints can yield the same probability, especially when algebraic identities such as (1−a)²−a²=1−2a apply. Verify all proposed intervals rather than accepting only a familiar form. A confidence-coefficient assertion is understood as the prescribed identity for all α in the stated range, not an accidental equality at one α.

similar_questions.prompt: For W~Exp(1), find P(−log(.9)<W<−log(.1)).
similar_questions.solution: The survival difference is .9−.1=.8.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the probability with both these bounds doubled.
similar_questions.solution: The difference is .9²−.1²=.81−.01=.8. Thus the doubled bounds give the same .8 coverage.

hints: The expected uniform minimum and maximum are a+(b−a)/(n+1) and a+n(b−a)/(n+1).
Use the stated completeness and sufficiency with the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem.
questions.solution: EX̄=θ₁, proving A. E X_(1)=θ₁−θ₂+2θ₂/(n+1), so E(X̄−X_(1))=θ₂(n−1)/(n+1), refuting B. The maximum expectation is θ₁+θ₂−2θ₂/(n+1); therefore the midpoint has mean θ₁ and the range has mean 2θ₂(n−1)/(n+1). Both estimators in C,D are unbiased functions of the given complete sufficient pair. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem makes each the unique UMVUE of its corresponding parameter. Thus A,C,D hold.
questions.theory: For n iid uniform observations on (a,b), rescaling to (0,1) gives expected minimum 1/(n+1) and expected maximum n/(n+1), obtainable from their beta order-statistic distributions or survival integrals. Consequently the expected range is (b−a)(n−1)/(n+1), so the raw range underestimates interval length. In a location-and-half-width parameterization, the midpoint of extremes is unbiased for the center. A sufficient statistic retains all parameter information in the factorized likelihood, and completeness means no nonzero integrable function of it has expectation zero for every parameter. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem states that an unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic is the uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator. Here completeness is supplied by the question, so it can be used directly after checking unbiasedness.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=4 uniform observations on (0,10), find expected range.

similar_questions.prompt: For uniform (μ−s,μ+s), find an unbiased half-width estimate from extremes when n=3.
similar_questions.solution: The expected range is 2s·2/4=s. Thus the range itself is unbiased for s, agreeing with factor (n+1)/(2(n−1))=1.

questions.prompt: Xᵢ are iid with density (1/(2θ))exp(−|x−θ|/θ), θ>0. Let Uₙ=ΣXᵢ/n, Vₙ=ΣXᵢ²/n and Sₙ²=Σ(Xᵢ−Uₙ)²/(n−1), n≥2. Which hold?
hints: This is Laplace with location θ and scale θ.
To disprove completeness, combine Vₙ and Uₙ² so that their expectations cancel.
questions.solution: For Laplace(location θ,scale θ), EX=θ and Var X=2θ², so EX²=3θ². Hence EUₙ=θ, proving A, while ESₙ²=2θ², refuting B. By the law of large numbers Vₙ→3θ², proving C. Also EUₙ²=θ²+2θ²/n=(n+2)θ²/n. Therefore g(Uₙ,Vₙ)=Vₙ−[3n/(n+2)]Uₙ² has expectation zero for every θ, but is not almost surely zero: the continuous full-support sample can have observations near a nonzero common value, where the expression is nonzero for n≥2. This integrable nonzero function disproves completeness, so D fails.
questions.theory: A Laplace distribution with location μ and scale b has density exp(−|x−μ|/b)/(2b), mean μ, variance 2b², and finite moments of every order. Its scale parameter is not its standard deviation. The usual sample variance with denominator n−1 is unbiased for the population variance. The law of large numbers makes a sample second-moment average consistent for EX², so a suitable known factor can convert it into a parameter-square estimator. Completeness of a statistic means every integrable function of it with expectation zero for all parameter values must vanish almost surely. One nontrivial zero-mean function disproves completeness. Comparing expectations of a sample second moment and squared sample mean often supplies such a function, because the latter includes the mean square plus the mean's sampling variance.

similar_questions.prompt: For Laplace(μ,b), find EX².
similar_questions.solution: EX²=Var X+(EX)²=2b²+μ².

similar_questions.prompt: For iid mean μ,variance σ², compute E(X̄²).

questions.prompt: One observation X has density θe^{−θ(x−1)} for x>1,θ>0. Test θ=1 against θ≠1. Which hold?

options.A: The likelihood is maximized at θ=1/(x−1).
options.C: The likelihood-ratio test rejects if (x−1)e^{−x}<k for some k>0.
options.D: The likelihood-ratio test rejects if x>c for some c>1.

hints: Write t=x−1>0 and maximize θe^{−θt}.
The likelihood ratio t e^{1−t} is small at both t near zero and large t.
questions.solution: Log likelihood is logθ−θt, with derivative 1/θ−t and negative second derivative −1/θ². The maximum is at θ=1/t and equals e^{−1}/t, proving A,B. The likelihood ratio is e^{−t}/(e^{−1}/t)=te^{1−t}=e²(x−1)e^{−x}. Thus rejection for a sufficiently small ratio is equivalent to C with a rescaled positive threshold. The ratio increases to its maximum at t=1 and decreases thereafter, tending to zero at both endpoints 0 and infinity. A nontrivial two-sided likelihood-ratio test therefore has two rejection tails, not just x>c, refuting D.
questions.theory: A likelihood-ratio test compares the maximum likelihood under the null with the unrestricted maximum, rejecting when their ratio is small. For one exponential-rate observation shifted by a known amount, maximization is done in the rate parameter, and the log likelihood is concave. A two-sided alternative often leads to a statistic that is small for both unusually short and unusually long observed waiting times. Multiplying a test statistic by a positive constant does not change the rejection region after adjusting the cutoff. The ratio's shape, not merely its expression, determines whether rejection is one-sided or two-sided. Check the parameter space and the data support before differentiating; here x>1 ensures the finite positive maximum θ=1/(x−1).

similar_questions.prompt: For one Exp(rate θ) observation t=2, find its MLE.
similar_questions.solution: The log likelihood logθ−2θ has score 1/θ−2, so the MLE is 1/2 and maximum likelihood e^{−1}/2.

similar_questions.prompt: For the ratio r(t)=te^{1−t}, locate its maximum.
similar_questions.solution: r′(t)=e^{1−t}(1−t), so it increases for t<1, decreases for t>1, and has maximum 1 at t=1.

questions.prompt: Independent samples X₁,…,X₇ and Y₁,…,Y₉ have continuous shift distributions F(x−μ),F(x−θ), with unique medians μ,θ. Let Rᵢ be Yᵢ’s rank in the combined sample and T=Σᵢ₌₁⁹Rᵢ. For testing μ=θ against μ>θ, which hold?

options.B: A right-tailed T test is appropriate.

hints: There are 16 ranks, and the largest nine are 8 through 16.
Under the null labelled ranks are exchangeable; under the alternative the Y sample tends smaller.
questions.solution: The maximal sum is 8+9+⋯+16=9(8+16)/2=108, not 115. Under μ>θ, the X observations are shifted right relative to Y, so Y ranks tend lower; rejection should be left-tailed, not right-tailed. Under H₀ each labelled rank is uniform on 1,…,16, with mean 17/2, so E T=9·17/2=153/2=76.5, not 76. Finally P(R₁=1)=1/16, and conditional on that R₉ is equally likely to occupy any of the other 15 ranks, giving joint probability 1/(16·15)=1/240. Only D holds.
questions.theory: The Wilcoxon rank-sum statistic sums the combined ranks belonging to one of two independent samples from continuous distributions, so ties occur with probability zero. Under the null of identical distributions, every allocation of ranks to sample labels is equally likely; each labelled observation has expected rank (N+1)/2, and two labelled ranks are uniformly distributed over distinct ordered pairs. The maximum sum of m selected ranks uses the top m ranks. Under a location-shift alternative, the direction of rejection depends on which sample's ranks are summed: if the other sample shifts upward, the summed sample's ranks become smaller. Rank tests are distribution-free under the null but their tail direction still requires interpreting the parameter inequality. Exact half-integer expectations should not be rounded in mathematical claims.

similar_questions.prompt: For sample sizes 3 and 4, sum the four second-sample ranks. Find its null mean.
similar_questions.solution: There are N=7 ranks with mean 4 each. The rank sum has expectation 4·4=16.

similar_questions.prompt: For two labelled observations among 10 exchangeable ranks, find P(first rank2,second rank7).
similar_questions.solution: The first event has probability 1/10 and the second conditional probability 1/9, so the joint probability is 1/90.

questions.prompt: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid N(θ,1). Which Bayes-estimator claims hold?

options.A: θ̂=ΣXᵢ/(n+τ²) for prior N(0,1/τ²), squared-error loss.
options.B: θ̂=ΣXᵢ/(n+τ²) for prior N(0,τ²), absolute-error loss.
options.C: θ̂=ΣXᵢ/(n+1/τ²) for prior N(0,1/τ²), absolute-error loss.
options.D: θ̂=ΣXᵢ/n for Jeffreys prior, squared-error loss.

hints: Posterior precision is likelihood precision n plus prior precision.
Squared loss uses the posterior mean; absolute loss uses the median, which equals the mean for a normal posterior.
questions.solution: With prior variance v, posterior precision is n+1/v and mean m=ΣXᵢ/(n+1/v). The posterior is normal, so mean and median coincide. For v=1/τ², m=ΣXᵢ/(n+τ²), proving A and refuting C. For v=τ², m=ΣXᵢ/(n+1/τ²), so B is false. For the normal location model with known variance, Fisher information is constant in θ, making Jeffreys prior flat. The posterior mean is X̄, proving D. Claims B,C fail as general formulas, although special τ values could make their denominators coincide.
questions.theory: A Bayes estimator minimizes posterior expected loss. Under squared-error loss the minimizer is the posterior mean; under absolute-error loss it is a posterior median. A normal posterior is symmetric, so these two estimators coincide. Normal likelihood with known variance and normal prior is conjugate: posterior precisions add, and the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the data mean and prior mean. A prior variance v contributes precision 1/v, so reciprocal-variance notation must be handled carefully. Jeffreys prior is proportional to the square root of Fisher information; for an unrestricted normal mean with known variance it is constant, giving the sample mean under squared loss. An estimator formula is a general claim in the hyperparameter, not an accidental equality for one value.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=2, prior θ~N(0,4), and observations 2,4 with variance1, find posterior mean.
similar_questions.solution: Data sum is 6 and total precision 2+1/4=9/4. Mean is 6/(9/4)=8/3; posterior variance is 4/9.

similar_questions.prompt: For a posterior N(3,2), give Bayes estimators under squared and absolute loss.
similar_questions.solution: The posterior mean and median are both 3, so both losses give estimate 3.

questions.prompt: Data have x=(−2,−1,0,1,2), yᵢ=xᵢ². Fit least-squares lines with and without intercept. Which hold?

options.A: Both lines have the same slope.
options.B: Both models have the same intercept.
options.C: The model with intercept passes through an observed point.
options.D: The model without intercept passes through an observed point.

hints: Symmetry makes Σx=Σx³=0.
The mean y is 2, while the no-intercept fitted line must pass through the origin.
questions.solution: Σx=0,Σx²=10,Σxy=Σx³=0, and ȳ=10/5=2. With intercept the slope is Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)²=0 and intercept 2, giving ŷ=2. Without intercept, the slope is Σxy/Σx²=0 and the implicit intercept is zero, giving ŷ=0. A holds and B fails. Observed y values are 4,1,0,1,4, none 2, so C fails. The no-intercept line passes through the observed point (0,0), proving D.
questions.theory: In simple least-squares regression with an intercept, the fitted slope is the centered cross-product divided by the centered x sum of squares, and the intercept is ȳ−β̂x̄. The fitted line always passes through the sample centroid, but need not pass through any individual observed point. Without an intercept, the fitted line is constrained to pass through the coordinate origin and its slope is the uncentered ratio Σxy/Σx². Symmetry of predictor values around zero often makes sums of odd powers vanish. If the response is an even function, such as x², that symmetry can make both fitted slopes zero while their intercepts differ. Distinguish the sample centroid from an observed data point, and use the correct centered or uncentered formula for the fitted model.

similar_questions.prompt: Fit a line with intercept to x=−1,0,1 and y=1,0,1.
similar_questions.solution: The slope is zero by symmetry and intercept is 2/3. The centroid lies on the line, but none of the three data points does.

similar_questions.solution: Slope is (1·2+2·2)/(1²+2²)=6/5. The line ŷ=1.2x does not pass through either observation.

options.C: Under the restrictions the residual sum of squares has σ²χ²_{n−3} distribution.
options.D: The unrestricted residual sum of squares has noncentral σ²χ²_{n−4} distribution.

questions.theory: A general linear hypothesis imposes q independent linear restrictions on regression coefficients. Under iid normal errors and a full-rank design, the full-model residual sum of squares divided by σ² is central chi-square with n−p degrees of freedom, where p counts all parameters including the intercept. The increase in residual sum of squares from q valid restrictions is independent central chi-square with q degrees, leading to an F_{q,n−p} test. The restricted model has p−q parameters and residual degrees n−p+q when the null is true. Under a false restriction its residual sum can become noncentral, but the correctly specified full model's residual remains central. Construct the restriction matrix by expanding the proposed reduced predictors and comparing their coefficients.

similar_questions.solution: Full residual degrees are n−5, reduced residual degrees n−2, and the extra residual sum has 3 degrees of freedom.
