questions.prompt: A positive-definite covariance matrix is [[1,ρ,ρ],[ρ,1,ρ],[ρ,ρ,1]]. Which hold?

options.B: The first principal component can explain only 32% of total variation for some ρ.
options.C: The second principal component can explain more than 32% of total variation for any ρ.
options.D: The first principal component has variance 1+2ρ for any ρ.

hints: The eigenvalues are 1+2ρ and 1−ρ with multiplicity two.
Principal components are ordered by decreasing eigenvalue, which changes at ρ=0.
questions.solution: The covariance matrix is (1−ρ)I+ρJ. Its eigenvalues are 1+2ρ on the all-ones direction and 1−ρ on its two-dimensional orthogonal complement. Positive definiteness requires −1/2<ρ<1, so −.47 is allowed, proving A. Total variance is 3, and the largest of three eigenvalues is at least their mean 1, so the first component explains at least 1/3>32%, refuting B. The second eigenvalue is always 1−ρ, whose explained fraction exceeds .32 only when ρ<.04; for instance at ρ=.5 it explains 1/6, refuting the literal “for any ρ” in C. When ρ<0 the largest eigenvalue is 1−ρ rather than 1+2ρ, refuting D. Thus A alone is true under the printed universal wording.
questions.theory: Principal component analysis diagonalizes a covariance matrix and orders components by decreasing variance, namely its eigenvalues. The total variance is the trace, and each component's explained fraction is its eigenvalue divided by that trace. An equicorrelation matrix in dimension d has eigenvalue 1+(d−1)ρ in the all-ones direction and 1−ρ with multiplicity d−1 on the orthogonal complement. Positive definiteness requires both types positive. Their ordering depends on the sign of ρ; a named formula for one eigenvalue does not automatically give the first principal component for every parameter value. The largest eigenvalue is at least the average, giving a universal lower bound 1/d for the first explained fraction. Distinguish an existential “for some” from a universal “for any” when evaluating possible percentages.

similar_questions.solution: Eigenvalues are .2,1.4,1.4. The first component has variance1.4, not .2, and explains1.4/3 of the total.

questions.prompt: A block design has incidence matrix N=[[1,1,1,0],[1,1,0,1],[1,0,1,1],[0,1,1,1]]. Which hold?
hints: Each block contains three of the four treatments.
Every treatment pair occurs together in two blocks; compare incidence with proportional row and column totals for orthogonality.
questions.solution: There are v=4 treatments and b=4 blocks. Every column sum is k=3<4, so the design is incomplete. Every row sum is r=3, and every distinct row pair has inner product λ=2; hence it is a balanced incomplete block design. All treatment pairs co-occur, so the concurrence graph is connected. More explicitly NNᵀ=I+2J and the treatment information matrix is C=3I−(1/3)NNᵀ=(8/3)I−(2/3)J, of rank 3=v−1. Orthogonality of treatment and block effects would require nᵢⱼ=rᵢkⱼ/N_total=9/12=3/4 for every cell, whereas entries are 0 or1. Thus D is false and A,B,C hold.
questions.theory: The incidence matrix of a binary block design records which treatment appears in each block. Row totals are treatment replications, and column totals are block sizes. A design is incomplete when blocks omit some treatments. A balanced incomplete block design has constant replication r, constant block size k, and constant concurrence λ for every pair of distinct treatments. Connectedness means all treatment contrasts are estimable; it can be tested by a connected concurrence graph or a treatment information matrix of rank v−1. Orthogonality of treatment and block effects is a different property: incidence must be proportional to the row and column totals after centering, corresponding to treatment/block independence. Balance does not imply orthogonality. Check both matrix dimensions and whether the design is binary before interpreting entries.

similar_questions.prompt: Four blocks each omit one of four treatments. Find v,b,r,k,λ.
similar_questions.solution: v=b=4, each treatment appears in3 blocks so r=3, each block has k=3, and each pair is absent only from two blocks, giving λ=2.

similar_questions.prompt: A complete block design has each of three treatments in each of two blocks. Is it connected and orthogonal?
similar_questions.solution: All treatment pairs co-occur, so it is connected. Every incidence entry is1, equal to r_i k_j/N=2·3/6=1, so treatment and block effects are orthogonal.

questions.prompt: Two parallel components have independent lifetimes Xⱼ exponential with mean1/j, j=1,2. Let R,h be system reliability and hazard. Which hold?
hints: A parallel system survives while at least one component survives.
Its lifetime is the maximum; use h=−R′/R and E T=∫₀∞R.
questions.solution: Rates are1 and2. The system fails by time t only if both components fail, so R=1−(1−e^{−t})(1−e^{−2t})=e^{−t}+e^{−2t}−e^{−3t}, proving A. Its expected lifetime is1+1/2−1/3=7/6, refuting B. Hazard h=(e^{−t}+2e^{−2t}−3e^{−3t})/(e^{−t}+e^{−2t}−e^{−3t})=(e^{2t}+2eᵗ−3)/(e^{2t}+eᵗ−1). At t=1 this is C. At t=3 the correct numerator is e⁶+2e³−3, differing from D, which is false.
questions.theory: Reliability R(t)=P(T>t) is the survival probability of a lifetime. A series system fails when its first component fails, so its lifetime is a minimum; a parallel system fails only when all components fail, so its lifetime is a maximum. Independence makes the probability of all component failures the product of their failure probabilities. For a continuous lifetime, hazard is f(t)/R(t)=−R′(t)/R(t), and the expected nonnegative lifetime equals the integral of reliability. Exponential mean and rate are reciprocals. Even when components have constant hazards, a parallel system's hazard generally varies with time, because the surviving system may consist of different combinations of active components. Use inclusion–exclusion for its reliability and differentiate the resulting expression carefully.

similar_questions.prompt: Two independent Exp(1) components run in parallel. Find mean system lifetime.
similar_questions.solution: Reliability is2e^{−t}−e^{−2t}; integrating gives2−1/2=3/2.

similar_questions.prompt: The same components run in series. Find reliability and mean.
similar_questions.solution: Both must survive, giving e^{−t}e^{−t}=e^{−2t}. The system is Exp(2) with mean1/2.

questions.prompt: An M/M/1 queue has arrival rate3 and exponential service times with mean1/9. Let Pₙ be the long-run probability of n customers in the system. Which hold?

options.C: The average number in the system is1.
options.D: The average time in the system is1/6.

hints: The service rate is9, so utilization isρ=3/9.
Use Pₙ=(1−ρ)ρⁿ, L=ρ/(1−ρ), W=1/(μ−λ).
questions.solution: λ=3,μ=9 andρ=1/3<1, so a stationary distribution exists. P₀=1−ρ=2/3, refuting A. P₁=(2/3)(1/3)=2/9, proving B. Mean number L=ρ/(1−ρ)=(1/3)/(2/3)=1/2, refuting C. Mean system time W=1/(μ−λ)=1/6, proving D; Little's law checks L=λW=3/6=1/2. System time includes both waiting and service.
questions.theory: An M/M/1 queue has Poisson arrivals with rate λ, independent exponential service times with rate μ, and one server. The stable case requires utilization ρ=λ/μ<1. Its number-in-system stationary distribution is geometric, Pₙ=(1−ρ)ρⁿ, obtained from birth–death balance equations. The mean number is L=ρ/(1−ρ), and mean total time is W=1/(μ−λ). Little's law L=λW connects these steady-state quantities. Waiting time excludes the service duration and equals W_q=W−1/μ, while system time includes it. A stated service mean1/μ must be inverted to obtain the service rate. Confusing idle probability1−ρ with utilizationρ or average queue length with average system population leads to different answers. These formulas assume an unlimited waiting room.

similar_questions.prompt: For arrival rate2 and service rate5, find idle probability and mean system time.
For those rates, find mean number and waiting time excluding service.
similar_questions.solution: L=λW=2/3. W_q=1/3−1/5=2/15; mean queue length is λW_q=4/15.
